To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the flux of cosmic rays with energies above 1E19 eV is about one third the flux predicted by the GZK cutoff theory, that the spectrum of cosmic rays with these energies is consistent with a power-law with an index of 3.0 ± 0.1, and that the composition of cosmic rays at these energies is consistent, within the uncertainties, with a mixture of protons and heavier nuclei.
HiRes has measured the energy spectrum of cosmic rays in the energy range 10^17 to 10^20 eV, and that there is a significant change in the slope of the spectrum at an energy of 5.7x10^19 eV.

the HiRes experiment has observed the first cosmic ray with an energy greater than 1020 eV and that the energy spectrum of cosmic rays above 5x1019 eV is well described by an exponential power law with a spectral index of -2.69 ± 0.02.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of UHECR, which are the highest energy cosmic rays known to exist.
the detection and measurement of the highest energy particles in the Universe.
the measurement of the flux of UHECR and the determination of their mass composition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HiRes has not found any evidence for a flux suppression at energies above 10^19 eV.
HiRes data are consistent with a single power law with a spectral index of -2.7.
the HiRes results are consistent with an isotropic flux of cosmic rays with a spectral index of -3.3 ± 0.1 and with a cutoff energy of 4.2 ± 0.6 EeV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the HiRes experiment has the capability of detecting and measuring the properties of UHECR.
we have measured the cosmic ray energy spectrum to energies of 10^20 eV and found it to be consistent with a power law with a slope of -3.3.
the HiRes experiment has been running successfully for the last 10 years and has collected data that is being analyzed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy spectrum of cosmic rays extends to above $10^{20}$ eV and that the spectrum is not a simple power-law, but has a feature around $10^{19.5}$ eV.
HiRes has measured the energy spectrum of UHECR up to 100 EeV (100 EeV = 10 ^{20} eV).
the flux of the UHECR is consistent with a power-law spectrum with an index close to −2 and the spectrum does not show any evidence of cutoff.
